title: Autoimmune epilepsy due to N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor antibodies in a child: a case report
case_prompt:
A previously healthy 5-year-old Sri Lankan boy presented with a 2-week history of recurrent seizures manifesting as staring episodes with behavioral arrest, some associated with retching, vomiting, and tachycardia. Between seizures, his behavior fluctuated between normal, irritable, and somnolent. He was afebrile, had no meningeal signs, and neurologic examination—including cranial nerves, motor, sensory, and cerebellar testing—was normal. Glasgow Coma Scale was 15/15.

Initial laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 11.3×10^3/µL with a normal differential, C-reactive protein <5 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 10 mm/hour, calcium 9.2 mg/dL, magnesium 1.9 mg/dL, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, normal renal and liver function (SGPT 14 U/L; SGOT 33 U/L; urea 14 U/L; creatinine 36 µmol/L), and normal thyroid hormones (T3 3.44 ng/dL; T4 1.2 ng/dL). 

Electroencephalography revealed intermittent theta and delta slowing over the right temporal and occipital regions; video EEG captured seizures with bilateral background attenuation evolving to fast activity and rhythmic theta over the right temporal and frontal regions. Brain CT and MRI were normal. 

Because of concern for infection, lumbar puncture was performed: CSF showed 22 lymphocytes/mm^3, 1 polymorph/mm^3, protein 30 mg/dL, glucose 3.9 mmol/L; bacterial antigens and cultures were negative, and HSV PCR was negative. Stool cultures were also negative.

He was empirically treated with intravenous cefotaxime and aciclovir (both discontinued after negative CSF results) and started on phenobarbitone (20 mg/kg IV), levetiracetam (up to 30 mg/kg/day), carbamazepine (up to 18 mg/kg/day), and clobazam (5 mg/day) orally. Seizure frequency initially decreased to 10–15 brief seizures per day but then escalated to 30–40 per day despite escalating ASMs. 

Further workup showed a serum lactate of 1.2 mmol/L. Serologic tests for antinuclear, thyroglobulin, and thyroid‐peroxidase antibodies were negative. Facilities for advanced metabolic or genetic epilepsy panels were unavailable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious encephalitis was excluded — “CSF analysis did not show a pleocytosis...; bacterial antigens were negative, and culture yielded no growth. Herpes simplex viral screen was negative.”  
2. Structural lesion (eg, focal cortical dysplasia) was excluded — “MRI of brain reviewed carefully remained normal without evidence of focal cortical dysplasia, and cortical or subcortical hyperintensities.”  
3. Metabolic or genetic epilepsy was considered but not confirmed — “Serum lactate level was 1.2 mmol/L. Facilities for advanced metabolic screening or genetic panels for epilepsy were unavailable.”  
4. Autoimmune epilepsy was suspected based on clinical features — “Features that would suggest an autoimmune etiology in epilepsy include young age at onset... poor response to ASM, and negative brain imaging.”  
5. NMDAR‐antibody epilepsy was confirmed by serology — “Examination of paired serum and CSF revealed presence of N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antibodies in serum but not in CSF.”
